name: Zane Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, of course. I love this kind of thing, actually. I talk about AI all the time and my partner Sam is sick of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do a mix for a big city agency: day calls three days a week, and two night sits, where I stay over with someone who can't be left alone. My regular night is with Mr Ferreira, who has Parkinson's and falls if he gets up for the toilet without help. I speak Spanish at home, so the agency sends me to a lot of the Spanish-speaking families, and I use an AI app every day to translate medication leaflets and to tidy my care notes, because my writing isn't great. I left school at sixteen and I'm still slow on things like catheter care, so I watch the senior carers a lot. What I love is the night sits, honestly, the quiet and the stories at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That would surprise me, because I already use it every day. But okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post that it was oversold but still useful, because it is, for me. At work I'd tell the others to keep using the translation and notes stuff anyway. I'd say the real problem in care was never technology, it's pay and staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. People keep getting older, the agency can't hire fast enough, and I get more night sits than I can take. Rent in the city is brutal, but Sam and I split it and I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the apps. I'd do the catheter and PEG feeding training this year so I can take the better-paid complex care shifts. And I'd keep pushing the union to get night sits paid properly, because at the moment we get a flat rate that works out under the hourly minimum if the client wakes up a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm, really. A bit disappointed, because I was curious what was coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the flat rate for night sits works out under the hourly minimum. How often does that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one night in three with Mr Ferreira, when he's up four or five times. On a night sit you're awake all night and paid as if you slept. The union reps are on it, and I've given them my diary of wake-ups as evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's struggling at work, even without AI changing anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older carers who drive. Fuel's gone up and the mileage rate hasn't. I take the bus and the night bus, so it doesn't hit me the same.

say: AI was **oversold**, but the translation and notes tools are still **useful** for carers.
The real problem in care was never technology; it's **pay and staffing**.
think: I'd be fine, because people keep ageing and I get **more night sits** than I can take.
City **rent is brutal**, but my partner and I split it and I have four months saved.
do: Take **catheter and PEG** training this year for complex care shifts.
Give the union his **diary of wake-ups** to fight the night-sit flat rate.
Keep using **AI apps** for translation and care notes.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **disappointed** because he was curious what was coming.
S0.quote: On a night sit you're awake all night and paid as if you slept.
fieldNote: Uses AI **daily already**, so a plateau only disappoints his curiosity.
His real grievance is the **night-sit flat rate**, and he's collecting evidence for the union.
Feels **secure** because demand outpaces hiring and he takes buses, not a car.

steps.text: Complete catheter and PEG feeding training this year
Hand the union a diary of night-sit wake-ups
Keep translating leaflets and tidying notes with AI apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I actually expect. Thinking stuff first, robots slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: care workers should be first in line to get the good tools, not last. At work I'd show people how I do my notes by voice, because half of them are still typing with one finger. Online I'd say the savings should go into wages, not shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The paperwork shrinks, the rota gets smarter, and someone who can work with the new systems and also do a proper wash is worth more. I could see myself as the person who trains other carers on the tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this month if I can be the agency's digital champion, they've talked about it. I'd do an online course on care technology in the evenings, the free one from the college. I'd still do the complex care training, because hands are still the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit nervous for the office staff, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nervous for the office staff. Who exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemi, who does our scheduling, and the two women who check timesheets. If the software does rotas and checks hours, those three jobs probably become one. I'd hope the union gets them first dibs on new roles, like monitoring the sensors at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside for carers like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, if they use the time AI saves to squeeze in more calls instead of giving us longer visits. That's my one real fear. Technology is only as good as whoever's deciding what to do with the time.

say: Care workers should be **first in line** for good tools, not last.
Any savings from AI should go into **wages**, not shareholders.
think: It's **good for me**: less paperwork, a smarter rota and more value for mixed skills.
I could be the one who **trains carers** on the tablets.
do: Ask his manager this month to be the agency's **digital champion**.
Take the free college **care technology** course in the evenings.
Keep the **complex care** training going, because hands are still the job.
feel: **Excited**, with some nerves for the **office staff**.
S1.quote: Technology is only as good as whoever's deciding what to do with the time.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as a **step up**, mixing digital skills with hands-on care.
His one fear is AI time savings used to **squeeze in calls**.
Thinks of colleagues by name and wants the union to give them **first dibs** on new roles.

steps.text: Apply this month to be the agency's digital champion
Take the free college care technology course in the evenings
Teach colleagues voice-dictated care notes on the agency tablets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's different. 2028 for the thinking, 2031 for robots that can do what I do. That's very soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for care workers now, not in 2030: paid retraining, and rules so robot companies can't just undercut everyone. I'd want the union in the room with the government, and I'd be loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the agency office is gone by 2028 and there'd be a short window where people like me run the robots. But robots good enough by 2031 means there aren't many of those jobs. One supervisor for twenty robots, maybe. I'd want to be that one supervisor, and so would everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd get onto any robot or sensor pilot the agency runs and make myself the person they ask. I'd use the two years before AGI to do a proper qualification, maybe assistant practitioner or occupational therapy assistant, something the robots support instead of replace. I'd stop the gym membership and push savings from four to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The kind where I'm moving fast so I don't have to sit with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone would want that supervisor job. What if you don't get it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lean on the language thing. A lot of my families want someone who speaks Spanish and knows how their grandmother likes her coffee. Maybe there's a small business in that, families paying for a human visit on top of the robot care. I don't know if anyone could afford it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop talking about moving to the bigger place near the park until 2030. Sam's a teaching assistant, so the school might go AI too, so that's two of us. We'd need to plan together.

say: Care workers need a plan **now**: paid retraining and rules against **undercutting**.
The union belongs **in the room** with government, and I'd be loud online.
think: There'd be a **short window** where people like me run the robots.
One **supervisor for twenty robots** means few of those jobs, and everyone wants one.
do: Join every **robot or sensor pilot** the agency runs.
Start an **assistant practitioner** or OT assistant qualification before 2028.
Cancel the **gym** and push savings from four to six months.
feel: **Anxious**, and moving fast so he doesn't have to sit with it.
S2.quote: One supervisor for twenty robots, maybe. I'd want to be that one supervisor, and so would everyone else.
fieldNote: Even an early adopter sees **few winners**: one supervisor for twenty robots.
Looks to his **Spanish** and cultural knowledge as a possible paid niche.
Both incomes feel **exposed**, since his partner is a teaching assistant.

steps.text: Volunteer for every robot and sensor pilot at the agency
Start an occupational therapy assistant qualification before 2028
Cancel the gym and build savings to six months
Push the union to demand paid retraining for carers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. That's still fast but it's a career's worth of time for me to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can do it right, if we start now. I'd want the government and the union to set up proper training routes for carers, and I'd post about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd come out okay. Five years is time to get the occupational therapy assistant qualification and some experience with the sensor systems. By 2034 I'd want to be the one deciding how a robot fits into someone's home, not the one being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year, I'd start the qualification part-time and keep my night sits for money. I'd learn the robot and sensor platforms as they come out. I'd keep the savings at four months but put a bit toward course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like the start of a hard but doable climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the carers who don't move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what bothers me. Someone like Kofi, a guy I trained with, hates apps and won't do online courses. He's a better carer than me in the room, honestly. He needs somebody to sit next to him and show him, and I'd do that if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave care altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd change what I do inside it. I like old people, I like the night shifts. I just don't want to be the cheapest pair of hands when the machine is cheaper.

say: This is the version where we can **do it right**, if we start now.
Government and the union should set up **training routes** for carers.
think: Five years gives me time for an **OT assistant** qualification and sensor experience.
By 2034 I want to **decide how robots fit** into homes, not be replaced.
do: Start the **OT assistant** qualification part-time next year.
Keep **night sits** for income while studying.
Learn new **robot and sensor** platforms as they launch.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a **good way**, like the start of a hard but doable climb.
S3.quote: I just don't want to be the cheapest pair of hands when the machine is cheaper.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan a **move within care**, not out of it.
Worries most about **less adaptable colleagues** who are better carers in the room.
Would personally **coach** a reluctant colleague if given the chance.

steps.text: Start the part-time occupational therapy assistant qualification next year
Keep two night sits a week to cover rent while studying
Learn each new robot and sensor platform as it launches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. I'd be 37. That's plenty for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody has an excuse, and I'd push for the union to have a seat on whatever committee plans it. With friends I'd say I'm genuinely looking forward to some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. By 2036 I'd be qualified, with years of experience in care tech, and robots would be doing the lifting that wrecks carers' backs. I'd be the human part of the service, the person who knows the family and checks the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the OT assistant course in a year or two, not rush it. I'd keep using AI every day and maybe build a small side thing, helping Spanish-speaking families set up care tech for their parents at weekends. Savings stay at four months, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious. A little bit sad about the night sits disappearing, because I love them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots doing the lifting. Have you hurt your back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice already, and I'm 27. Mr Ferreira fell in the bathroom in March, and I got him up the wrong way because I panicked. A robot that does the hoisting properly would be a good thing for carers, not just bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two in the morning stuff. Mr Ferreira telling me about his brother's boat in the war. A robot will keep an old man safe at night, but it won't ask him about his brother's boat.

say: With ten years, **nobody has an excuse**, and the union needs a seat at the table.
I'm genuinely **looking forward** to some of it.
think: By 2036 I'd be **qualified** and experienced in care tech.
Robots would take the **lifting that wrecks** carers' backs.
do: Start the **OT assistant** course in a year or two, without rushing.
Build a weekend **side service** setting up care tech for Spanish-speaking families.
Keep savings at **four months** and use AI daily.
feel: **Calm and curious**, with some **sadness** about losing night sits.
S4.quote: A robot will keep an old man safe at night, but it won't ask him about his brother's boat.
fieldNote: He's hurt his **back twice** at 27, so he welcomes robots doing hoisting.
Sees himself as the **human part** of a mixed service.
His sadness is about **night-time conversations**, not money.

steps.text: Start the OT assistant course in a year or two
Offer weekend care-tech setup to Spanish-speaking families
Keep using AI tools daily in care notes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because 2031 is too soon for robots in care when nobody's trained and nobody's set rules. What would help is paid retraining for carers starting now, and the union getting a say in how robots come into homes, so it isn't just whatever's cheapest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many of us already use AI. Loads of carers use AI quietly to translate or write notes, and the bosses don't know. We're not as behind as people think.

headlineQuote: Loads of carers use AI quietly to translate or write notes, and the bosses don't know.
portrait: A 27-year-old **city care worker** doing day calls and night sits, often for Spanish-speaking families.

Strongly **pro-union**, collecting evidence against the night-sit flat rate.
Calm in AI Plateau and **excited** in Steady Disruption, seeing a role as digital champion.
Anxious only in **AGI by 2028**, when robot supervisor jobs would be few.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in care by 2031 come before training or rules.
